rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The declarative al-ḥamdu lillāh is preferable to ahmadu Allāh: it establishes praise as God’s right instead of reporting one speaker’s act.
rows.anchor: فثبت أن قوله الحمد لله أولى من قوله أحمد الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām in lillāh can signify fitting اختصاص, ownership, or power and dominion; each makes all praise belong to God.
rows.anchor: اللام في قوله الحمد لله يحتمل وجوها كثيرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ḥamdu lillāh has eight letters corresponding to Paradise’s eight gates; saying it with a pure heart merits those gates.
rows.anchor: الحمد لله ثمانية أحرف وأبواب الجنة ثمانية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One grammatical view makes definite al-ḥamd refer to a prior known instance, or otherwise to all praise to avoid ambiguity.
rows.anchor: إن كان مسبوقا بمعهود سابق انصرف إليه وإلا يحمل على الاستغراق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second grammatical view says the definite noun denotes only the essence or nature of praise, not universal scope.
rows.anchor: أنه لا يفيد العموم إلا أنه يفيد الماهية والحقيقة فقط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On either grammatical analysis, the phrase denies that anyone besides God is independently entitled to praise.
rows.anchor: فثبت على القولين أن قوله الحمد لله ينفي حصول الحمد لغير الله

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet is cited as saying that whoever does not thank people does not thank God; al-Rāzī answers that God is the true source of every human benefit.
rows.anchor: من لم يحمد الناس لم يحمد الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A human benefactor acts only because God creates the motive, the blessing, and the recipient’s capacity to benefit, so God is the true benefactor.
rows.anchor: كل من أنعم على غيره بإنعام فالمنعم في الحقيقة هو الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A giver who seeks reward, praise, repayment, or release from stinginess seeks compensation and is not the true benefactor; God gives from intrinsic fullness.
rows.anchor: كل من أنعم على الغير فإنه يطلب بذلك الإنعام عوضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every blessing is a possible existent brought into being by God, directly or through means; therefore praise for blessing belongs to God.
rows.anchor: كل نعمة فهي من الموجودات الممكنة الوجود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A complete blessing requires benefit, freedom from harm, and security from loss, and only God supplies all three conditions.
rows.anchor: النعمة لا تكون كاملة إلا عند اجتماع أمور ثلاثة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People cannot fully thank God because they cannot enumerate His countless blessings, as the Qur’an says.
rows.anchor: نعم الله على الإنسان كثيرة لا يقوى عقل الإنسان على الوقوف عليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ability, motive, and freedom from obstacles needed for gratitude are themselves gifts, so thanking them would require endless further thanks.
rows.anchor: إذا زال عنه العوائق والحوائل فكل ذلك إنعام من الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human conceptions of perfection never reach God’s greater perfection, so people cannot praise Him as He deserves.
rows.anchor: كل ما خطر ببال الإنسان من صفات الكمال والجلال فكمال الله وجلاله أعلى

rows.speaker: الواسطي
rows.claim: Al-Wāsiṭī calls gratitude shirk when a person imagines that his thanks can equal God’s blessings.
rows.anchor: وهذا معنى قول الواسطي الشكر شرك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because full gratitude is beyond human capacity, the verse states that all praise belongs to God rather than commanding people to praise Him.
rows.anchor: لم يقل احمدوا الله بل قال الحمد لله

rows.speaker: داود
rows.claim: David asks how he can thank God when even the ability to thank depends on God’s gift; God says recognizing that incapacity is gratitude according to one’s capacity.
rows.anchor: يا رب كيف أشكرك وشكري لك لا يتم إلا بإنعامك علي

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: A report says that when a blessed servant says al-ḥamdu lillāh, God tells the angels that the servant returned something priceless for an unvalued gift.
rows.anchor: إذا أنعم الله على عبده نعمة فيقول العبد الحمد لله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ḥamdu lillāh encompasses every praise uttered or possible from all creatures, prophets, angels, saints, scholars, and future inhabitants of Paradise.
rows.anchor: كل حمد أتى به أحد من الحامدين فهو لله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report’s expanded wording contrasts one immeasurable blessing with the servant’s boundless thanks in saying al-ḥamdu lillāh.
rows.anchor: قد أعطيته نعمة واحدة لا قدر لها فأعطاني من الشكر ما لا حد له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worldly blessings are finite, but the praise phrase is infinite; what remains after accounting for a finite blessing is endless, warranting eternal reward.
rows.anchor: غير المتناهي إذا سقط منه المتناهي بقي الباقي غير متناه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Existence is better than nonexistence, and every possible existent receives its existence from God; hence every creature receives His blessing and mercy.
rows.anchor: وجود كل شيء ما سوى الله تعالى فإنه حصل بإيجاد الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Praise precedes tasbīḥ because it includes transcendence and adds God’s beneficence, making Him beyond mere completeness.
rows.anchor: التحميد يدل على التسبيح دلالة التضمن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rationally, beneficence requires knowing every need, power to meet it, and freedom from need; divine beneficence therefore presupposes perfection without deficiency.
rows.anchor: كونه محسنا لا يتم إلا بعد كونه منزها عن النقائص والآفات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Praise thanks God for past blessings and brings future increase, as promised in the Qur’an; it closes barriers and opens the way to knowledge of God, hence the name al-Fātiḥa.
rows.anchor: أما تعلقه بالماضي فهو أنه يقع شكرا على النعم المتقدمة

rows.speaker: السري السقطي
rows.claim: Al-Sarī al-Saqaṭī spent thirty years seeking forgiveness for thanking God that his shop survived Baghdad’s fire while others’ homes and shops burned, since his happiness showed disregard for others.
rows.anchor: وقع الحريق في بغداد واحترقت الدكاكين والدور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase should be reserved for the best blessings: religious benefits outrank worldly ones, inner acts outrank bodily acts, and seeing a worldly benefit as the giver’s gift is nobler than treating it merely as a benefit.
rows.anchor: نعم الدين أفضل من نعم الدنيا لوجوه كثيرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says Adam’s first words were al-ḥamdu lillāh after he sneezed; the people of Paradise end with the same praise, so the world begins and ends with it.
rows.anchor: لما بلغ الروح إلى سرته عطس فقال الحمد لله رب العالمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī rejects supplying an unspoken command ‘say’: the phrase is already a complete assertion that praise belongs to God.
rows.anchor: قوله الحمد لله إخبار عن كون الحمد حقا له وملكا له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The assertion makes God intrinsically deserving of praise through His essence and acts, whether people praise Him or not; what is essential exceeds what depends on another.
rows.anchor: يدل على كونه تعالى مستحقا للحمد بحسب ذاته وبحسب أفعاله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Stating that praise is due, rather than directly commanding it, lets the obedient praise God while leaving the disobedient with a lesser offense than rejecting an order.
rows.anchor: فمن كان مطيعا حمده ومن كان عاصيا إثمه أقل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Jabriyya argue that if humans created faith, the human would deserve more praise for this noblest act than God; therefore God creates faith.
rows.anchor: لو كان الإيمان فعلا للعبد لكان استحقاق العبد للحمد أولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Jabriyya argue that Muslims praise God for the blessing of faith; if faith were a human act, praising God for it would wrongly credit Him with another’s act.
rows.anchor: أجمعت الأمة على قولهم الحمد لله على نعمة الإيمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Jabriyya argue that obligatory acts only avert blame and cannot earn praise, while voluntary grace would make God gain praise and thus be perfected by another.
rows.anchor: أداء الواجبات فإنه لا يفيد استحقاق الحمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They further argue that if God is praised intrinsically, no act causes that entitlement, so no duty, compensation, or reward is owed; if it is not intrinsic, God would depend on another.
rows.anchor: استحقاقه الحمد والمدح إما أن يكون أمرا ثابتا له لذاته

rows.speaker: الجبرية
rows.claim: The Jabriyya infer that faith too comes from God: all praise belongs to Him, praise follows blessing, and faith is the greatest blessing.
rows.anchor: الإيمان أفضل النعم فوجب أن يكون الإيمان من الله

rows.speaker: الجبرية
rows.claim: They argue that God’s self-praise, though blameworthy among people, shows divine acts cannot be judged by human standards and challenges Muʿtazilī principles.
rows.anchor: فلما بدأ كتابة بمدح النفس دل ذلك على أن حاله بخلاف حال الخلق

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Muʿtazila say absolute praise is deserved by one whose acts contain no evil, rulings no injustice, and judgments no oppression; they reject the Jabriyya picture of God creating disbelief then punishing it.
rows.anchor: المستحق للحمد على الإطلاق هو الذي لا قبيح في فعله

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: They argue that if a servant deserves God’s praise, the servant must be capable of action, contrary to determinism; if God praises Himself, that is also invalid, so the phrase only works on their doctrine.
rows.anchor: إن كان الأول وجب كون العبد قادرا على الفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Scholars disagree whether gratitude is owed by reason or only by revealed law; the latter cite the rule that punishment awaits a messenger and the removal of excuses by messengers.
rows.anchor: من الناس من قال : إنه ثابت بالسمع لقوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī argues that gratitude is due at all times, even before revelation: the verse makes praise God’s right without qualification and grounds it in His nurturing and mercy.
rows.anchor: يدل على ثبوت هذا الاستحقاق قبل مجيء الشرع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: True praise is any act expressing reverence for a benefactor: inward belief in perfection, spoken words of praise, or bodily deeds that express it; saying al-ḥamdu lillāh merely reports praise.
rows.anchor: حمد المنعم عبارة عن كل فعل يشعر بتعظيم المنعم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One group says God cannot command praise: if it repays a blessing, the command makes generosity transactional; if not, it is needless toil imposed on another.
rows.anchor: ذلك التحميد إما أن يكون بناء على إنعام وصل إليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same group says praise is useless to a God complete in Himself and that punishing people eternally for omitting a useless act would not befit the generous Lord.
rows.anchor: الكامل لذاته يستحيل أن يستكمل بغيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second group calls praise bad manners: the tiny thanks cannot match immeasurable blessings, recalling blessings distracts from knowing the giver, and praise for benefits seems self-interested.
rows.anchor: الاشتغال بالشكر لا يتأتى إلا مع استحضار تلك النعم في القلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only God is necessary in Himself; everything else is possible and is called the world because its existence points to God.
rows.anchor: العالم كل موجود سوى الله وسبب تسمية هذا القسم بالعالم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Possible existents divide into spatial bodies, attributes of bodies, and things neither; bodies include celestial spheres and scriptural entities, earthly elements and composites, while attributes comprise about forty genera.
rows.anchor: كل ما سوى الله تعالى إما أن يكون متحيزا وإما أن يكون صفة للمتحيز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The third class is spirits: lower spirits include good jinn and evil demons; higher ones are attached to celestial bodies or are holy, disembodied spirits.
rows.anchor: فهو الأرواح وهي إما سفلية وإما علوية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since possible beings need God to bring them into existence and preserve them, He is their deity as creator and their Lord as sustainer.
rows.anchor: هو الذي أخرجها من العدم إلى الوجود وهو رب العالمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Created nurturers seek their own profit, such as reward or praise, while God nurtures for the creatures’ benefit rather than His own.
rows.anchor: والقسم الثاني هو الحق سبحانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s nurturing does not diminish His store; unlike other givers, He gives from inexhaustible provision.
rows.anchor: وما ننزله إلا بقدر معلوم

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet is cited as saying that God loves those who persistently supplicate; no grading is stated.
rows.anchor: إن الله تعالى يحب الملحين في الدعاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God gives before being asked, nurturing a person as a fetus and protecting him before he can think or pray.
rows.anchor: أما الحق تعالى فأنه يعطي قبل السؤال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unlike human benefaction, God’s care never ends and reaches everyone.
rows.anchor: والحق تعالى لا ينقطع إحسانه البتة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The four motives for honoring someone map onto the verse: intrinsic perfection, beneficence, hoped-for future good, and fear correspond respectively to God, Lord, Merciful, and Master of Judgment.
rows.anchor: هذه الحالات هي الجهات الموجبة للتعظيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Embryonic development forms distinct bones, cartilage, ligaments, vessels, and senses, displaying God’s care; He gives hearing through bone, sight through fat, and speech through flesh.
rows.anchor: فسبحان من أسمع بعظم وبصر بشحم وأنطق بلحم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A seed’s shoot and roots develop in opposite directions, then produce branches, flowers, fruit, food, oils, and medicines; fine roots draw nourishment even through hard soil.
rows.anchor: الحكمة في كل هذه التدبيرات تحصيل ما يحتاج العبد إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God arranged night for rest and day for work, the sun and moon for timekeeping, stars for navigation, and earth and mountains for habitation; reflecting on nature reveals His providence.
rows.anchor: خلق الليل ليكون سببا للراحة والسكون وخلق النهار ليكون سببا للمعاش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sequence assigns praise to God, then names Him Lord of the worlds: Allah signifies necessary perfection, while Lord of the worlds shows that all else flows from His generosity, making Him beyond completeness.
rows.anchor: أن وجود كل ما سواه فائض عن تربيته وإحسانه وجوده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A Prophetic saying calls the human being God’s structure and curses whoever demolishes it; God guards people by night and day despite their sins.
rows.anchor: الآدمي بنيان الرب ملعون من هدم بنيان الرب

rows.speaker: القدرية
rows.claim: The Qadariyya argue that God would not truly be Lord if He created a disbeliever’s unbelief and then punished him, or commanded faith while preventing it.
rows.anchor: إنما يكون تعالى ربا للعالمين ومربيا لهم لو كان محسنا إليهم

rows.speaker: الجبرية
rows.claim: The Jabriyya answer that faith is the greatest blessing, so if it comes from God He is the Lord and benefactor of all.
rows.anchor: لما كان الإيمان أعظم النعم وأجلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Allah is nobler than Lord, although supplicants commonly call God ‘Lord’; al-Rāzī refers readers to his earlier discussion of the divine names.
rows.anchor: قولنا الله أشرف من قولنا رب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Raḥmān gives blessings of a kind servants cannot produce, whereas al-Raḥīm gives blessings of a kind they can produce.
rows.anchor: هو المنعم بما لا يتصور صدور جنسه من العباد

rows.speaker: إبراهيم بن أدهم
rows.claim: Ibrāhīm ibn Adham recounts a raven stealing a loaf and carrying it to a bound man, illustrating providential care.
rows.anchor: حكي عن إبراهيم بن أدهم أنه قال كنت ضيفا لبعض القوم

rows.speaker: ذو النون
rows.claim: Dhū al-Nūn recounts a scorpion riding a frog across the Nile, then killing a snake that threatened a sleeping youth, illustrating unseen protection.
rows.anchor: وروي عن ذي النون أنه قال : كنت في البيت إذ وقعت ولولة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A raven chick emerges naked and vulnerable; gnats feed it until it grows feathers and its mother returns, prompting the Arab prayer ‘Provider of the nestling in its nest’ and showing universal mercy.
rows.anchor: يا رزاق النعاب في عشه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Events may look merciful while harming in reality, like a parent neglecting a child, or appear painful while benefiting, like schooling a child or amputating a diseased hand.
rows.anchor: فالأبله يغتر بالظواهر والعاقل ينظر في السرائر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Trials and pain are ultimately wisdom and mercy: abandoning great good to avoid slight evil would be a greater evil, so the wise judge realities rather than appearances.
rows.anchor: إن ترك الخير الكثير لأجل الشر القليل شر كثير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Religious duties purify spirits from bodily attachments, while Hell redirects the wicked toward righteous action and toward God.
rows.anchor: المقصود من التكاليف تطهير الأرواح عن العلائق الجسدانية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses judged by outward appearances and objected to the boat, boy, and wall, while al-Khiḍr acted on hidden realities; disliked events may conceal divine wisdom and mercy.
rows.anchor: فاستنكر تخريق السفينة وقتل الغلام وعمارة الجدار المائل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Raḥmān is exclusive to God while al-Raḥīm can describe God or others; the lower name follows because people may hesitate to ask a great Lord for small needs.
rows.anchor: الرحمن : اسم خاص بالله والرحيم : ينطلق عليه وعلى غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adding al-Raḥīm invites requests for even ordinary necessities such as a sandal strap or cooking salt; a report says God told Moses to ask Him for salt and fodder.
rows.anchor: يا موسى سلني عن ملح قدرك وعلف شاتك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mary was saved from slander by one divine mercy; worshippers recite the two mercy names 34 times daily in prayer, so al-Rāzī hopes for their rescue from punishment.
rows.anchor: فلما صار ذكر الرحمة مرة واحدة سببا لخلاص مريم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is al-Raḥmān because He creates what humans cannot, transforming impure semen into a beautiful form; He is al-Raḥīm because He returns imperfect obedience as a perfect Garden.
rows.anchor: أنا رحمن لأنك تسلم إلي نطفة مذرة فأسلمها إليك صورة حسنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A story tells of a dying youth unable to utter the testimony because his mother, whom he had injured, refused to forgive him; when she relents at the threat of burning, his speech returns.
rows.anchor: اعتقل لسانه عن شهادة أن لا إله إلا الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mother’s limited mercy would not permit burning her son after carrying and nursing him, so God’s boundless mercy should not burn a believer who professed faith for seventy years.
rows.anchor: فالرحمن الرحيم الذي لم يتضرر بجنايات عبيده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the Prophet’s tooth was broken, he reportedly prayed for his people’s guidance; his mercy on earth and his concern for his community at resurrection show the effect of being sent as mercy.
rows.anchor: اللهم اهد قومي فإنهم لا يعلمون

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: Reports say the Prophet asked that his community’s accounting be in his own hands, yet he withheld funeral prayer for a debtor of two dirhams and removed ʿĀʾisha over the slander; one mercy cannot repair all creatures.
rows.anchor: اللهم اجعل حساب أمتي على يدي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God tells the Prophet to leave the servants to Him: the Prophet’s single mercy is finite, but God’s mercy is infinite and absorbs every creature’s finite sins.
rows.anchor: فرحمتي لا نهاية لها ومعصيتهم متناهية

rows.speaker: القدرية
rows.claim: The Qadariyya ask how God can be merciful if He creates people for eternal Hell, creates their disbelief and punishes it, or orders faith then blocks it.
rows.anchor: كيف يكون رحمانا رحيما من خلق الخلق للنار

rows.speaker: الجبرية
rows.claim: The Jabriyya argue that faith is the greatest mercy; if humans produced it, they rather than God would deserve the names al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm.
rows.anchor: أعظم أنواع النعمة والرحمة هو الإيمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mālik yawm al-dīn means Master of resurrection and recompense, when distinctions between good and evil, obedience and disobedience, must become manifest.
rows.anchor: قوله مالك يوم الدين أي مالك يوم البعث والجزاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If God left oppressors unpunished, that would imply incapacity, ignorance, or approval of injustice, all impossible; since full retribution is absent in this world, it must occur in the next.
rows.anchor: لما لم يحصل هذا الانتقام في دار الدنيا وجب أن يحصل في دار الأخرى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says a man enters Paradise for remembering God during a brief waking moment before sleep overcame him; God never sleeps and did not forget the praise.
rows.anchor: تقلبت من جنب إلى جنب ليلة كذا فقلت في خلال ذلك الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another report says a card bearing the testimony that there is no god but God outweighs a person’s good and bad deeds.
rows.anchor: فتأتيه بطاقة فتثقل ميزانه فإذا فيها شهادة أن لا إله إلا الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Duties owed to God rest on forbearance because He needs nothing, whereas people’s rights must be carefully avoided.
rows.anchor: حقوق الله تعالى فمبناها على المسامحة لأنه تعالى غني عن العالمين

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Abū Ḥanīfa carefully cleaned dirt from a Zoroastrian debtor’s wall rather than wrong him; moved by this care over a minor harm, the man converted, prompting reflection on divine justice.
rows.anchor: فأنا أبدأ بتطهير نفسي فأسلم في الحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers differ between Mālik, ‘Owner,’ and Malik, ‘King’; the first reading has an extra letter and thus more reward, and only God is the true owner of Judgment Day despite many kings there.
rows.anchor: اختلف القراء في هذه الكلمة فمنهم من قرأ مالك يوم الدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author favors Mālik because ownership enables disposal, can include kingship, and imposes deeper mastery: a slave is lower than a subject and cannot choose to escape ownership.
rows.anchor: فالملكية والمالكية قد تنفك كل واحدة منهما عن الأخرى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ownership entails more submission than kingship: a king must care for subjects, while a slave owes service and cannot act independently of the master’s permission.
rows.anchor: فعلمنا أن الانقياد والخضوع في المملوكية أتم منه في كونه رعية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Supporters of Malik say everyone owns something, whereas only the greatest person is king; the refuge chapter also uses Malik al-nās as the required reading, supporting kingship’s superiority.
rows.anchor: كل واحد من أهل البلد يكون مالكا أما الملك لا يكون إلا أعظم الناس وأعلاهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They also cite the refuge chapter’s wording Malik al-nās as proof that ‘King’ is the necessary reading there.
rows.anchor: لفظ الملك فيه متعين

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Supporters of Malik also prefer the shorter word because reciters may have enough time to finish it but not the longer Mālik; Abū ʿAmr is cited for this argument.
rows.anchor: الملك أولى لأنه أقصر والظاهر أنه يدرك من الزمان

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī answers that intending to recite Mālik is enough if death prevents completion, comparing it to a fasting intention made after sunset.
rows.anchor: إني أشرع في ذكر هذه الكلمة فإن لم أبلغها فقد بلغتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse’s kingship entails layered governance: kings over owners, angels over kings, and the King of Kings above angels, who speak or intercede only by permission.
rows.anchor: فسياسة الملوك أقوى من سياسة الملاك
